claims.statement: The panel kernel is assembled by exactly three functions that each return an unstarted cordis `Context`: `createKernel` (in-process assembly, no production caller, used by the offline kernel contract seam), `createDataplaneKernel` (four collection services for the utilityProcess child), and `createPanelKernel` (production main-process window/host assembly).

A kernel's services are only reachable after the caller awaits `ctx.start()`: production boot calls `await kernel.start()`, then `await kernel.panelData.whenReady`, then wires bridge IPC with `kernel.bridge`, and every kernel-level test brackets its body with `await ctx.start()` / `await ctx.stop()`.

`app/src/main/kernel.ts` must not import electron so that pure-Node vitest can load it; the Electron-only production assembly therefore lives in `panel-kernel.ts`, because the production port implementation `services/dataplane.ts` imports `utilityProcess` from electron at module scope, while all other Electron/native access is behind lazy `require()` calls with non-Electron fallbacks.

The data-plane child process has no Electron APIs available, so all Electron-resolved paths and roots are resolved in the main process and shipped to the child as a `DataplaneInit` bundle (desktop `roots`, `storeFile`, `docMaxRows`, `usageDir`).

In both main-process assemblies the `panelData` port implementation is registered immediately before `BridgeService` (the source comments call this a prerequisite of the bridge registration), and `PluginHostService` is always registered with a spread-in default of `roots: []` so an offline kernel installs no plugins and creates no plugin directory.

Only two services declare a cordis `static inject` list — `BridgeService` (clock, panelData, search, settings, focus, plugins) and `LocalPanelDataService` (clock, sessions, hardware, desktop) — while every other service receives its dependencies as constructor option bundles (`HardwareSources`, `DesktopDeps`, `UsageDeps`, `SearchDeps`, `FocusDeps`) whose real implementations are defaults and whose members are individually overridable; that bundle mechanism is what lets one assembly function swap in fake sources.

The usage-to-desktop recommendation edge is created by the assembly function as a closure over `ctx.usage?.iconScores(...)` that returns an empty map when the service is absent, so a kernel without the usage service degrades to the stable name order instead of failing; `ctx.usage` is typed optional for this reason.

`DataplaneService` signals snapshot arrival with the internal `dataplane/snapshot` event instead of calling the bridge directly, because `BridgeService` injects `panelData` and therefore does not exist yet while the port implementation is being constructed; a direct `ctx.bridge` access from that service trips cordis's unregistered-property warning.

The kernel owns this exact set of interval timers and defaults: panel push tick `DEFAULT_TICK_MS` = 1000 ms (createKernel, calling `bridge.tick()`), data-plane sample round `DEFAULT_TICK_MS` = 1000 ms (createDataplaneKernel, calling `sessions.refresh()` + `desktop.refresh()` + the `onSnapshot` sink), hardware sample `DEFAULT_HARDWARE_MS` = 1000 ms, usage collect `DEFAULT_USAGE_MS` = 2000 ms, usage prune `USAGE_PRUNE_MS` = 3_600_000 ms, and search pump `DEFAULT_SEARCH_INTERVAL_MS` = 50 ms.

Every kernel interval is guarded by a greater-than-zero check, so passing 0 installs no timer and lets a test drive the same work by hand; because the hourly prune timer is created inside the same branch as the usage collector, `usageIntervalMs: 0` disables both usage timers.

The production assembly installs no snapshot timer at all — `createPanelKernel` has exactly one interval, the 50 ms search pump — because in production the child's 1 s tick drives reflection into the panel by arriving as the `dataplane/snapshot` event; this is why `tickIntervalMs` exists in `KernelOptions`/`DataplaneKernelOptions` but not in `PanelKernelOptions`.

Kernel timer callbacks reach services through optional chaining, so a timer that fires after construction but before `ctx.start()` mounts the services is a no-op rather than a crash, and the genuinely optional `usage` service simply drops out of the tick.

Each kernel timer is cleared by a dispose handler registered next to it, and `ctx.stop()` additionally tears down service-owned resources: the desktop root watcher, the plugin directory watcher plus every installed plugin instance (disposed once), in-flight search generations, and the data-plane child together with its pending restart timer.

`PanelDataPort` has ten members and both implementations register under the same cordis service name `panelData`, with `ctx.panelData` typed as the port interface; `BridgeService` reads the clock/sessions/hardware/desktop snapshot sections and dispatches the desktop icon/launch/move/reset-layout actions only through that port, so it is independent of whether collection runs in-process or in a child process.

The in-process port resolves `whenReady` immediately and its `refresh()` drives sessions and desktop rescans, whereas the production port resolves `whenReady` on the child's first ready/snapshot message or after the 15 s `DEFAULT_READY_TIMEOUT_MS` timeout (which logs `dataplane-ready-timeout` and lets the panel start with an empty data plane) and its `refresh()` is deliberately a no-op.

In the production port, Electron-only capabilities stay in the main process: `icon()` uses a main-process `IconCache`, `launch()` is validated against the main process's own copy of the latest snapshot item pool before `shellOpen`, and only the two layout writes (`move`, `resetLayout`) are RPC to the child using a sequence number plus a pending-request map that is rejected when the child exits.

Data-plane child death is a degraded mode rather than a crash: pending RPCs are rejected, a restart is scheduled with `min(30_000, 1000 * 2 ** attempt)` backoff, the attempt counter resets when a message arrives, and on-disk state (layout placement, usage log) converges after restart while the hardware history ring restarts empty.

Kernel-level test coverage is split three ways: `tests/contract.spec.ts` creates the in-process kernel with all four interval options set to 0 and drives `ctx.bridge.tick()`/`ctx.search.tick()` by hand while asserting invoke responses and pushed events; `tests/services.spec.ts` runs snapshot-contract cases on the same zero-timer assembly plus bare-Context service tests; and `tests/dataplane-kernel.spec.ts` runs `createDataplaneKernel` in-process with real 10 ms timers and asserts the snapshot sections seen by the `onSnapshot` sink plus the desktop write path, with the child entry covered by the acceptance battery instead.

Timers that are not kernel-owned belong to their own layers and must not be attributed to the assembly functions: the window host's 25 ms hotzone cursor poll, the Win+D restorer's 250 ms poll with a 1500 ms debounce, the plugin watcher's 300 ms event-storm settle debounce (created only when roots are non-empty and watching is on), and `DataplaneService`'s one-shot 15 s readiness timeout and 1 s-to-30 s restart backoff timeouts.
